Like the Vps33 template complex, the Munc18-1 template complex is thought to represent a rate-limiting intermediate in the process of SNARE assembly (20). CryoEM structures of Munc18-1:synaptobrevin:syntaxin-1 (19) differ markedly, however, from the Vps33/16:Nyv1:Vam3 structure presented above (Fig. 3). For Vps33, the assembly nucleus is centered around the −2 layers of the two SNARE motifs, where short α-helices form and pack against the distal portion of the helical hairpin. By contrast, the Munc18-1 assembly nucleus is centered around the −5 layers of the SNARE motifs, which do not interact with the helical hairpin but instead form a four-helix bundle with two short helices (Hd and He) contributed by the N-terminally adjacent linker region of syntaxin-1 (19) (Fig. 3, A and C). Thus, whereas the Vps33 template complex nucleates SNARE assembly nearer the center of the two SNARE motifs, the Munc18-1 template complex nucleates it nearer their N-termini. Indeed, only the N-terminal layers of the Munc18-1-bound SNAREs, beginning near the artificial crosslink at layer −6 and extending to the −4 layer, are reasonably well aligned (19) (Fig. 3B); beyond this, the absence of an inter-helix break near the 0 layer prevents synaptobrevin from interacting significantly with either the Munc18-1 helical hairpin or the other SNARE (Fig. 3A). Finally, as observed for the assembly nucleus of Vps33, the layer residues within the Munc18-1 assembly nucleus are partially buried against the templating helices and must presumably rotate outward for Qb/Qc-SNARE binding (Fig. 3C). For Munc18-1, as for Vps33, these rearrangements are likely facilitated by the flexibility of the assembly nucleus ((19) and Fig. 2B).

### Vps33/16:Nyv1 structure

Two lines of evidence suggest that Nyv1 binding precedes Vam3 binding in Vps33-catalyzed SNARE assembly. First, the SNARE motif of Nyv1 binds more tightly than Vam3 to Vps33, suggesting that the latter interaction is more transient (15). Second, experiments using reconstituted proteoliposomes suggested that HOPS binds Nyv1 on one membrane before engaging Vam3 on the other (24). To better elucidate the structure of the Nyv1-only intermediate, we sought to determine a Vps33/16:Nyv1 structure in which Nyv1 H1 was not involved in crystal packing. To achieve this goal, we used the above-described Vps16 construct to generate a new 2.9-Å Vps33/16:Nyv1 structure (PDB: 9ZCT; Table S1) in the same crystal form as the template complex structure (9ZCS). We also revisited our previously reported Vps33/16:Nyv1 structure (5BV0 (15)), adding residue assignments for Nyv1 residues 165 to 179 and yielding extended resolution and improved refinement statistics; this updated structure was redeposited with PDB accession code 9ZBE (Experimental procedures; Table S1).

Overall, the new Vps33/16:Nyv1 structure (9ZCT) is very similar to the updated structure (9ZBE) but lacks the crystal contact involving Nyv1 H1; without this crystal contact, H1 is pivoted 15° around its C-terminus and is about four residues shorter at its N-terminus (see Fig. 2C). Strikingly, the new Nyv1-only complex (9ZCT) is virtually identical—except of course for the absence of Vam3—to the template complex (9ZCS), with an overall rmsd of 0.4 Å. Thus, at least at these resolutions (2.9–3.2 Å), the conformation of the initial Nyv1-only assembly intermediate is not significantly perturbed by the subsequent binding of Vam3 to form the template complex.

### Nyv1 alanine-scanning mutagenesis

To validate the new Nyv1-only structure (9ZCT), and elucidate the basis for its stability, we conducted alanine scanning mutagenesis across the entire ordered region of the Nyv1 SNARE motif and used a Vps33 pulldown assay to assess the Vps33:Nyv1 interaction (Figs. 4A and S2). The impact of alanine substitutions on Vps33 pulldown efficiency correlated with the sequence conservation scores, calculated using Consurf, of the Nyv1 residues that were replaced (R2 = 0.2) (Fig. 4, B–D). Notably, this was true even though the Nyv1 conservation scores presumably reflect not just Vps33 binding but also any subsequent roles in SNARE assembly and/or function. One third (12 out of 37) of the alanine mutants displayed a statistically significant reduction in binding to Vps33 (p < 0.05; n = 3) (Fig. 4A). Mutations in Nyv1 H2 were the most deleterious, with Vps33 binding virtually eliminated by I184A (+1 layer), L187A (+2 layer), V188A, and L194A (+4 layer) (Fig. 4, A and E). Other mutations in the C-terminal half of the Nyv1 SNARE motif significantly weakened binding, including K190A, T191A (+3 layer), and F201A (+6 layer). Consistently, truncation of Nyv1 residues C-terminal of the +5 layer reduced, but did not abolish, binding (25), and a Vps33 mutation designed to weaken Nyv1 H2 binding (G338E) compromised vacuole fusion in vivo and proteoliposome fusion in vitro (15).

We were especially interested in the impact of alanine substitutions in Nyv1 H1, both because side chain assignments had previously been unknown and because this helix plays a key role in nucleating SNARE assembly. None of the substitutions abolished Vps33 binding altogether, but binding was significantly compromised by Nyv1 M170A (−3 layer), I174A, E175A, L177A (−1 layer), and L178A. Notably, these are precisely the residues that contact the helical hairpin (Fig. 4E), strongly validating the new Vps33/16:Nyv1 structure (PDB: 9ZCT). Finally, despite exceptionally high sequence conservation across all four families of R-SNARE, alanine mutation of the 0-layer R180 or the adjacent glycine residue G181 did not cause a statistically significant reduction in Vps33 binding (Fig. 4, A–D). Thus G181, like R180, appears to have another role.

## Discussion

SM proteins are thought to increase the rate and fidelity of SNARE assembly by forming SM:R-SNARE:Qa-SNARE template complexes (1, 2, 3). In this work, we report the structure of the SNARE-binding module of HOPS/CORVET, containing the SM protein Vps33, bound simultaneously to the R-SNARE Nyv1 and the Qa-SNARE Vam3. As previously predicted (15), short α-helices N-terminal to the 0 layer of each SNARE motif align on the distal portion of the Vps33 helical hairpin, forming a nucleus for SNARE complex assembly. This configuration implies that the SNARE complex nucleates in the vicinity of the −2 layer rather than zippering from N- to C-terminus. The helices then must propagate both N- and C-terminally, driven by the coupled binding and folding of the Qb- and Qc-SNAREs. The force of zippering is expected to break the more stable interactions between the C-terminal halves of the SNARE motifs and Vps33, liberating the assembled SNARE complex from the SM template.

In the template complex, many of the residues that form the core of the assembled SNARE complex are partly or completely buried against Vps33. How then do the Qb- and Qc-SNAREs recognize the R- and Qa-SNARE to initiate assembly? Several lines of evidence suggest that the assembly nucleus is flexible enough for Nyv1 H1 and Vam3 Hf to sample other conformations, including conformations more closely matching the one they adopt within the fully assembled SNARE complex. First, relatively high B-factors imply that Nyv1 H1 and Vam3 Hf, along with the distal portion of the Vps33 helical hairpin, are more mobile than the rest of the template complex, although to what extent this reflects mobility of individual helices relative to the others is unknown. Indeed, the SNARE assembly nucleus might be even more flexible in solution than in the crystals, which contain a small crystal contact that could constrain the mobility of the hairpin (Fig. S1). Second, Nyv1 H1 and Vam3 Hf each bury a modest 320 Å2 of surface-accessible area against the helical hairpin, and the interface between Nyv1 and Vam3, at 200 Å2, is even smaller (Table S2). Thus, the helix-helix interactions within the SNARE assembly nucleus are likely metastable. Third, Nyv1 alanine-scanning mutagenesis demonstrates that H1 contributes less to Vps33 binding than H2. This suggests that Nyv1 remains bound to Vps33 via H2 while H1 explores alternate conformations. Taken together, our findings suggest that the assembly nucleus is not a static template perfectly aligned for further assembly, but instead a dynamic feature balancing a reasonably stable SM:SNARE complex with accessibility for Qb- and Qc-SNARE interactions.

Structural studies of two different SM proteins, Vps33 ((15) and this work) and Munc18-1 (19), reveal SNARE assembly nuclei consisting of small, flexible four-helix bundles. Despite these commonalities, however, the Vps33 and Munc18-1 assembly nuclei differ in major respects. First, the regions within the SNARE motifs that contribute to the assembly nuclei are different: nearer the 0 layers for Vps33, nearer the N-termini for Munc18-1. Second, the remaining helices come from different sources: the SM helical hairpin for Vps33, the Qa-SNARE linker for Munc18-1. These differences may reflect the distinctive contexts in which the two template complexes form and function. For Munc18-1, the Qa-SNARE binds first, forming a stable Munc18-1:syntaxin-1 complex. Subsequent binding of the R-SNARE requires the synaptic vesicle tethering protein Munc13-1, which engages the syntaxin-1 linker to remodel the SM:Qa-SNARE complex (14, 26, 27). Thus, the participation of the Qa-SNARE linker in the SNARE assembly nucleus might be a specialization related to its interaction with Munc13-1. Furthermore, conformational changes in the template complex, potentially involving the linker, are required for subsequent ternary SNARE complex formation, and these changes limit the rate of SNARE assembly at high Qbc-SNARE concentrations (21). Vps33-dependent SNARE assembly also has unique features: it initiates with R-SNARE binding, and it occurs in the context of large membrane tethering complexes containing additional SNARE-binding sites (24, 25, 28, 29, 30); whether, and how, these unique features affect SNARE assembly intermediates is unknown. Finally, it remains possible that Munc18-1 and/or Vps33-mediated SNARE assembly involve multiple template complex conformations. Indeed, cryoEM identified two different conformational populations for the Munc18-1 template complex (19), and perhaps a Vps33-like conformation is also part of the native assembly pathway. Likewise, the Vps33-mediated assembly pathway could include one or more Munc18-1 template complex-like conformations.

It also remains possible that one or both template complex structures were influenced by the experimental strategies needed to obtain them. While the Munc18-1 template complex contained the entire cytoplasmic domain of the Qa-SNARE (19), the Vps33 template complex contained only its SNARE motif, and we were unable to crystallize complexes containing larger portions. Consequently, our Vam3 construct lacked the Qa-SNARE linker that contributed to the SNARE assembly nucleus in the Munc18-1 complex, as well as the Habc domain, which is required for Munc18-1 (but not Vps33) template complex formation (20, 31). Conversely, the Munc18-1 template complex contained an engineered disulfide bond within the SNARE assembly nucleus, as noted above, as well as mutations in the syntaxin-1 linker and the Munc18-1 helical hairpin (19). Additional work will be needed to further elucidate structural distinctions between the two template complexes and their mechanistic and physiological significance.

The region of Nyv1 that is most important for Vps33 binding, layers +1 to +4, varies significantly among R-SNAREs, suggesting that it plays a role in SM:R-SNARE binding specificity. A 5-residue stretch within this region, with the consensus sequence LVDKT (layers +2 to +3; residues 187–191), may be particularly important, as judged by conservation within and between the four families of R-SNAREs (Fig. 4D). Consistent with this hypothesis, Nyv1 L187 and V188 are essential, and K190 and T191 are important, for Vps33 binding (Fig. 4A). The corresponding residues are almost identical (LVAKS) in the Ykt6 family of R-SNAREs, which also bind Vps33, but not in the Sec22 (MSEMS) family, which do not (25). The selectivity with which Vps33 binds R-SNAREs containing LVAKT/S provides a plausible mechanism for excluding synaptobrevin-family R-SNAREs (LQDKA) from Nyv1-family SNARE complexes, despite the coexistence of both R-SNARE families within the endolysosomal system (32, 33).

Our results contribute to a better structural and mechanistic understanding of two sequential intermediates in HOPS-catalyzed SNARE assembly, in which the R-SNARE and then the Qa-SNARE bind Vps33 to form a template complex. Further work will be needed to establish the structural roles of other factors—including Rab proteins, specific lipids, and the geometric constraints imposed by the HOPS/CORVET complexes and the apposed membranes—in SM-chaperoned SNARE assembly.

## Experimental procedures

### Recombinant protein production

T. thermophilum genes were identified and cloned as described previously (15, 22). Deletions and point mutations were introduced using the Q5 site-directed mutagenesis protocol (New England Biolabs). Full-length His7-Vps33 and Vps16 residues 520 to 791 were overproduced using a co-expression plasmid in BL21-CodonPlus bacteria in Luria-Bertani broth. Cells were grown at 37 °C to an OD600 of 0.4 to 0.6. We then reduced the temperature to 16 °C and induced expression with 0.5 mM IPTG for 18 h. Cells were pelleted and resuspended in lysis buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 250 mM NaCl, 1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT)) supplemented with 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonylfluoride, 10 μg/ml DNase (Roche), and 1 mg/ml lysozyme. Cells were lysed with an Emulsiflex-C5 homogenizer (Avestin) and clarified by centrifugation at 30,000g. Clarified lysate was loaded onto His60 Ni Superflow Resin (ClonTech), washed (50 mM Tris, pH 7.4, 250 mM NaCl, 5 mM β-mercaptoethanol (BME), 40 mM imidazole, pH 8.0), and eluted (50 mM Tris, pH 7.0, 50 mM NaCl, 5 mM BME, 300 mM imidazole, pH 8.0). Protein was further purified using a CaptoS or HiTrapSP cation exchange column followed by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) with a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) equilibrated in SEC buffer (20 mM Tris, pH 7.4, 250 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT). Fractions containing Vps33/16 were pooled, concentrated, flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80 °C.

Nyv1 residues 148 to 212 and Vam3 residues 181 to 229 were expressed with N-terminal His7-MBP tags and purified as above with the following differences. N-terminal tags were removed by overnight digestion at 4 °C with TEV protease immediately following the Ni2+-NTA affinity chromatography step. For Vam3, anion exchange chromatography was performed instead of cation exchange, using a MonoQ column (Cytiva). Finally, no DTT was included in the chromatography buffers due to lack of Cys residues in the SNARE motifs.

Vps33 for binding assays was expressed with a N-terminal His7-MBP tag and purified as with Vps33/16 with the following differences. Ni-NTA elution and ion exchange buffers contained 50 mM MES, pH 6.0 instead of Tris. N-terminal tags were removed by overnight digestion at 4 °C with TEV protease immediately following the Ni2+-NTA affinity chromatography step with dialysis into a low salt buffer (50 mM MES, pH 6.0, 50 mM NaCl, 5 mM BME). Cation exchange was performed on a HiTrapSP column (Cytiva).

### Crystallization, data collection, and refinement

Vps33/16:Nyv1:Vam3 crystals were grown at 20 °C using the hanging drop vapor diffusion method with a 1:1 (v/v) mixture of protein (4 mg/ml Vps33/Vps16 with a 3-fold molar excess of Nyv1 and a 4-fold molar excess of Vam3) and precipitant solution (0.1 M HEPES, pH 7.5, 0.5 M LiCl, 13% PEG8000, 1 mM DTT). Vps33/16:Nyv1 crystals were grown with the same methodology, excluding Vam3 and using a precipitant solution of 0.1 M HEPES, pH 7.5, 0.55 M LiCl, 11% PEG8000, 1 mM DTT. Diffraction data were collected at beamlines 17-ID-1 (AMX) and 17-ID-2 (FMX) at the National Synchrotron Light Source II at Brookhaven National Laboratory. Data were processed using XDS (34) and scaled with AIMLESS (35).

Vps33/16:Nyv1:Vam3 and Vps33/16:Nyv1 structures were determined by molecular replacement using PDB entry 4JC8 for a model of Vps33 and entry 4KMO for a model of Vps16. While Vps33 was largely unchanged, Vps16 required modification at its N- and C-termini reflecting the new construct and crystal packing environments. Models were iteratively rebuilt in Coot (36) and refined in Phenix.refine (37). The Vps33/16:Nyv1:Vam3 and Vps33/16:Nyv1 structures have been deposited in the PDB with entries 9ZCS and 9ZCT, respectively.

We also revised our previously-deposited model (5BV0) for Vps33/16:Nyv1, adding residue assignments for Nyv1 residues 165 to 179 (helix H1) based on consideration of side-chain local environments and yielding improved refinement statistics. As noted previously, crystal packing causes Nyv1 H1 to adopt a mixed conformation, interacting either with the Vps33 helical hairpin of the same complex or the Vps33 helical hairpin of a crystallographically adjacent complex. We therefore modeled residues 165 to 179 at 50% occupancy. The reinterpreted Vps33/16:Nyv1 structure has been deposited in the PDB with ID 9ZBE.

### Pull-down assays

Wild-type and mutant Nyv1 proteins were expressed as His7-MBP fusion proteins in BL21-CodonPlus bacteria and lysed as described above. Ni-NTA Spin columns (Qiagen) were equilibrated with 600 μl lysis buffer and loaded with 6 × 600 μl clarified lysate from 250 ml of bacterial culture. Columns were washed with 2 × 600 μl wash buffer (lysis buffer plus 20 mm imidazole, pH 8.0) and then incubated for 30 min with 600 μl blocking buffer (wash buffer plus 0.05% Tween-20 and 1% casein). Columns were washed with 600 μl wash buffer and incubated 30 min with Vps33, purified as above and diluted to 0.2 mg/ml in sample buffer (wash buffer plus 0.05% Tween-20). Columns were washed with 600 μl wash buffer and then eluted with 600 μl elution buffer (wash buffer with 500 mM imidazole, pH 8.0). All steps were performed at 4 °C.

Samples were visualized by SDS-PAGE gels stained with GelCode Blue Safe Protein Stain (Thermo Scientific) and imaged using a ChemiDoc gel imager (BioRad). Binding was quantified by densiometric analysis in Fiji. Binding differences were determined using a Welch’s ANOVA test with Dunnett’s T3 multiple comparisons test. Correlation between binding and conservation was determined using linear regression. Statistical analysis was performed in GraphPad Prism (Dotmatics).

### Sequence conservation analysis

At least 13 representative SNARE proteins for each class were manually selected from species representing all six eukaryotic supergroups and aligned using Clustal Omega. HMMER was used to generate HHM profiles for each class and search against the UniProt Reference Proteomes database. After sequences found in more than one SNARE class were removed, the total number of sequences in each class were: 997 synaptobrevin, 1478 Nyv1/VAMP7, 1326 Ykt6, 1706 Sec22. Residue conservation was determined for each class using ConSurf (38).

## INTRODUCTION

The term “Ozempic face,” characterized by sunken cheeks, sagging skin, and hollow eyes, has gained significant media attention alongside a surge in popularity of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA). Following a 700% rise in GLP-1RA prescriptions among patients without diabetes, approximately one in eight US adults report having used a GLP-1RA medication [1, 2]. Concurrent with national data indicating a rapid increase in GLP-1RA adoption, Google search volume for “Ozempic Face” nearly equaled that of “Ozempic weight loss” in 2024, revealing a prevalent association between GLP-1RA use and potential unintended dermatologic outcomes in the public’s perception [3]. Although existing literature suggests that GLP- 1RAs may improve inflammatory skin conditions, contemporary social discourse highlights the potential adverse effects correlated with GLP-1RA use, including skin sagging, hair loss, facial volume loss, and reduced muscle strength. Despite growing media interest regarding aesthetic concerns linked with GLP-1RA-driven weight loss, patient-reported data on the dermatologic impacts of GLP-1RA use and large-scale studies investigating these outcomes remain limited. We sought to address this research gap and characterize key features of the public commentary concerning potential dermatologic side effects of GLP-1RAs by surveying patients on weight management regimens inclusive of GLP- 1RA medications.

## METHODS

Survey Development and Administration

This institutional review board-approved study utilized a voluntary anonymous survey, developed from questions generated by dermatologists and obesity medicine physicians. These questions were based on recurring patient concerns identified in clinical practice and qualitative interviews with patients. Data collected included current weight management therapy, encompassing medication type, dosage and duration, along with pretreatment and current body weight. Participants responded to qualitative inquiries regarding dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic impacts associated with weight management therapy, such as changes in preexisting skin conditions and perceived changes in skin, hair, nails, facial volume, and muscularity. The voluntary anonymous survey was composed of 19 questions. Response choices were in multiple choice format and included current weight management therapy, medication dosages, medical conditions, and more (Supplementary Material). Inclusion criteria were adults enrolled in a telemedicine program receiving medical weight management therapy. Exclusion criteria were incomplete survey responses, missing weight data, and duplicate responses. Patients on prescribed weight management regimens from a virtual cardio–kidney–metabolic treatment program completed the survey, and responses (n = 1226) were captured in a RED- Cap database. No identifiable patient data were obtained. This study does not include any new investigations of human subjects or animals.

Ethical Approval

This article does not contain any new studies with human participants or animals performed by any of the authors. This study was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki of 1964 and its later amendments. The Massachusetts General Brigham Institutional Review Board has approved this study,

With respect to skin sagging and decreased facial volume, the percentage-point discrepancy peaked in the 10–20% weight loss category (skin sagging: 32 percentage points, 47% in GLP-1RA versus 15% in nonGLP1RA; decreased facial volume: 19 percentage points, 38% in GLP-1RA versus 19% in nonGLP1RA) and narrowed in the > 20% weight loss category (skin sagging: 12 percentage points, 71% in GLP1-RA versus 59% in nonGLP1RA; decreased facial volume: 11 percentage points, 52% in GLP-1RA versus 41% in nonGLP1RA). In the 10–20% weight loss category, the skin may have a variable ability to retract, contributing to a peak in the percentage-point discrepancy. In the > 20% weight loss category, the skin may have less ability to retract among both GLP-1RA and nonGLP1RA weight management groups, explaining the narrowing of the percentagepoint discrepancy in that weight loss category. The relative impact of GLP-1RA use on patientreported skin sagging and facial volume loss may decrease with more substantial weight loss, with less of an impact from treatment modality. Aesthetic concerns may be proactively addressed through holistic, interdisciplinary care. For example, identification of potential adverse dermatologic effects linked to GLP-1RAs allows for early clinical implementation of preventative skincare, hair growth, and musclebuilding regimens, and potentially also facial

and body skin tightening and contouring strategies to effectively support patients navigating GLP-1RA treatment regimens. Skin sagging, particularly of the arms, abdomen, and thighs, was the most frequently reported concern among survey respondents (37.7%). Rapid weight loss depletes elastin, collagen, and subcutaneous fat, limiting the skin’s adaptive capacity to retract and conform to a new body shape [4, 5]. Increased skin laxity manifesting as folds and wrinkles may detract from the aesthetic benefits of weight loss and contribute to functional challenges that reduce overall patient satisfaction. Nonsurgical treatments, such as radiofrequency (RF), high‐intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), fractional lasers, and fractional RF microneedling, may be utilized to promote skin elasticity and structural renewal by stimulating collagen and elastin protein synthesis [6–8]. Facial volume loss was the second most frequently reported concern among survey respondents (29.2%). Depletion of subcutaneous fat most commonly impacts the midface, temples, and periorbital region, contributing to a hollowed, aged appearance [5]. In addition, previous research suggests that GLP-1RAs reduce production of protective cytokines, increase oxidative stress, and promote adipose-derived stem cell death [9]. Dermatologic treatments, including dermal fillers and biostimulatory agents (e.g., poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) and calcium hydroxylapatite), may prevent progressive facial volume loss by promoting natural collagen production [10]. Hair loss was reported nearly as frequently as facial volume loss (28.9%) among survey respondents. While there is evidence to suggest that GLP-1RAs may improve scalp perfusion and mitigate inflammatory fibrosis in central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia, other literature hypothesizes that GLP-1RA use may disrupt the follicular cycle, contributing to the development of telogen effluvium (TE) [11, 12]. Nutritional deficiencies that arise from caloric restriction during weight management treatment may further accelerate hair loss. TE may be a transient condition, especially with adequate nutritional support, as seen in patients in other scenarios of rapid or significant weight loss such as bariatric

surgery [13]. In addition, GLP-1RA medications may be helpful in settings where scalp inflammation and hormonal imbalances contribute to alopecia [14]. Although alopecia often improves in patients with TE following nutritional recovery and weight stabilization, research among GLP-1RA users is limited. Strategies to stimulate hair growth include protein and micronutrient optimization, topical or oral minoxidil utilization, 5a-reductase and androgen receptor blockade in patients with androgenetic alopecia, and platelet-rich-plasma (PRP) therapy [15–17]. Approximately one quarter of survey respondents (24.1%) reported worsened skin quality, including skin dryness, wrinkles, and/or fine lines. Reduced protein and micronutrient intake resulting from GLP-1RA-driven hunger suppression may contribute to these effects. Dehydration and micronutrient deficiencies, such as the depletion of water-soluble vitamins including vitamin C and copper, can compound to impair collagen synthesis, barrier function, and elasticity [18–20]. Strategies to preserve skin quality include micronutrient optimization, retinoid application, antioxidant utilization, and microdepot hyaluronic acid injections (FDA-approved to enhance skin smoothness) as well as energybased procedures, such as lasers, microneedling, and radiofrequency [21]. Optimizing adequate hydration helps prevent dehydrated skin, which is a temporary lack of moisture leading to tightness, flaking, and a dull appearance of the skin. However, hydration alone is not a sufficient strategy to manage dry skin, which primarily lacks oil, not water. A combined approach composed of internal hydration alongside topical interventions such as humectants and moisturizers can address dry or dehydrated skin [22]. A notable proportion of survey respondents (17.9%) reported reduced muscle strength, particularly in the arms, thighs, and legs. Lean tissue loss may be intensified by rapid weight loss, inadequate protein intake, and insufficient resistance training [23, 24]. Acute muscle depletion exposes patients to elevated risks of sarcopenia, functional decline, and reduced longevity, as low thigh muscle strength correlates with poor survival. Optimizing nutrition and prioritizing resistance exercise are essential for maintaining muscle strength and function. These

strategies may be supplemented by energy-based technologies, such as high-intensity focused electromagnetic (HIFEM) therapy, to increase muscle tone [23, 25, 26].

Weight‑Loss‑Mediated versus Drug‑Specific Effects

This study cannot determine whether patientreported aesthetic changes resulted from the direct pharmacologic effects of GLP-1RAs or from the rate and extent of weight loss itself. Similar findings of skin laxity, facial volume loss, and hair shedding following substantial weight loss through bariatric surgery and other nonGLP-1 weight management interventions have long been recognized. Therefore, these outcomes may primarily indicate a physiologic consequence of adipose tissue loss rather than a finding associated with GLP-1RA medications. However, improvements in inflammatory dermatoses may result directly from immunomodulatory effects of GLP-1RAs in addition to weight reduction. Further studies comparing GLP-1 and nonGLP-1 therapies among patients with comparable weight loss are necessary to differentiate between these mechanisms. Patients with certain preexisting skin conditions, including psoriasis, acne, eczema, hidradenitis suppurativa, acanthosis nigricans, hirsutism, seborrheic dermatitis, and skin tags, reported improvement on at least one GLP-1RA medication. For example, a patient with a history of hidradenitis suppurativa for over a decade refractory to adalimumab and sekucinumab reported reduced disease flares following the initiation of semaglutide (Fig. 2). Existing literature suggests that GLP-1RAs improve inflammatory dermatoses through direct immunomodulation (e.g., inhibition of proinflammatory cytokine secretion) [27]. Adipocytes secrete proinflammatory cytokines known as adipokines that amplify systemic inflammation. Existing literature has established that weight loss and improved insulin regulation may attenuate preexisting skin conditions [28]. Owing to the antiinflammatory role of GLP-1RA medications, patients may experience dermatologic disease flares following the discontinuation of GLP-1RA treatment (Fig. 3).

Given that our survey results suggest a positive correlation between adverse dermatologic outcomes and percentage body weight loss, further investigation of how these changes manifest, specifically whether certain effects are linked directly to GLP-1RA use versus to the extent or rate of weight loss, is imperative. Such research is especially critical considering recent genetic evidence that variation in GLP- 1RA target genes contributes to interperson variability in response. A new study by Su et al. has identified a missense variant in GLP1R that is strongly associated with increased weight loss efficacy of GLP-1 medications. In addition, the study identified associations linking variation

in both “GLP1R” and “GIPR” to GLP-1RA medication side effects [29]. These findings suggest that an individual’s unique genetic makeup may enhance their therapeutic response to GLP-1RAs both in terms of weight loss and side effects, laying the foundation for dermatologic precision medicine in the context of weight management treatment. Supposing that certain dermatologic outcomes are associated with weight loss achieved with GLP-1R-inclusive treatment regimens, future research may reveal correlations with specific genetic polymorphisms. Moreover, the extent of the dermatologic effects identified in this study may be significantly lower than in unsupervised settings. With one in four US adults on weight management medications reporting receiving them from a source other than their primary care provider or trained specialist (e.g., online provider, medical spa, etc.) in 2024, there may be incidence of additional dermatological changes beyond those reported by patients receiving monitored care [30]. Because the survey was cross-sectional and relied on patient-reported outcomes, causality cannot be established. This study design does not allow distinction between effects attributable to GLP- 1RAs themselves and effects attributable to the degree or rapidity of weight loss. Other limitations of this study include its voluntary survey design, potential recall bias, and a study population largely consisting of white, female telemedicine patients, which may restrict the scope of application. Furthermore, data collected did not include the rate of weight loss, leaving its impact on dermatologic outcomes undetermined. These findings highlight the need for future dermatologist-assessed studies to further understand the patient experience and clarify the incidence, mechanisms, and long-term dermatologic effects associated with GLP-1RA therapy.

## CONCLUSIONS

Precision medicine is an innovative approach to healthcare that tailors prevention, diagnosis, and treatment for patients based on their unique genetic makeup, environment, and lifestyle. Recent genetic evidence suggesting that variation in GLP-1RA target genes contributes to interperson variability in response regarding both weight loss and side effects,

together with patient-reported dermatologic outcomes (stratified by percent body weight loss since treatment initiation and categorized by weight management regimen) identified in our study, establish the groundwork for precision dermatology within the context of weight management. By identifying patients that may be predisposed to certain dermatologic effects through genetic analysis, physicians may develop tailored treatment approaches that optimize patient outcomes while preventing unwanted results from the beginning of weight management treatment. Precision medicine can thus permit early implementation of personalized interventions and strategies for patients who may be genetically susceptible to adverse dermatologic effects. This study highlights the importance of collaborative, interdisciplinary care between obesity medicine physicians and dermatologists within the weight management landscape. For patients with inflammatory skin conditions in addition to obesity or diabetes, clinically coordinated GLP-1RA treatment can be utilized to achieve both health improvements and dermatologic improvement. Furthermore, dermatologic guidance is essential to address adverse aesthetic and dermatologic outcomes associated with GLP-1RA therapy. Precision dermatology encourages early implementation of a tailored, holistic treatment approach that supports skin and hair health as well as facial volume and muscle strength in patients on GLP-1RAs, especially among those who may be genetically predisposed to unwanted dermatologic effects. Combining patient-reported dermatologic outcomes with genetic evidence linked to GLP- 1RA response variability informs personalized medicine at the intersection of dermatology and clinical weight management. This interdisciplinary work contributes to the growing body of knowledge around precision medicine and supports the development of proactive, personalized treatment approaches to optimize holistic patient outcomes. Further investigation of the mechanisms responsible for dermatologic effects linked to GLP-1RA therapy is imperative for future refinement of GLP-1RA-associated precision dermatology.

## Abstract

As glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have become increasingly central to obesity care, calls for protocols to mitigate or prevent potential aesthetic and muscle sequelae have emerged.

This study aimed to to evaluate patient-reported concerns regarding aesthetic and muscle-related changes during pharmacologic weight management, particularly among individuals treated with GLP-1RAs, and to highlight potential strategies to address these effects.

An institutional review board–approved anonymous survey of 1,226 patients receiving pharmacologic weight management through a national telemedicine platform assessed patient-reported dermatologic, aesthetic, and muscle-related outcomes. Survey findings were analyzed and supplemented with a targeted PubMed literature review to develop a practical management framework.

Over 60% of participants reported concerns including skin laxity, facial volume loss, hair shedding, worsened skin quality, and reduced muscle strength. These concerns increased with greater weight loss and were more common among GLP-1RA users, who generally experienced greater weight reduction than non-GLP-1RA users.

Limitations of this study include the voluntary survey design, potential selection and recall bias, and a study population largely consisting of White, female telemedicine patients, which may limit generalizability. Rate of weight loss was not captured, leaving its impact on outcomes uncertain.

As unwanted aesthetic and muscle effects can undermine treatment adherence, a holistic approach including nutrition, strength preservation, and – when appropriate – aesthetic and regenerative therapies – could promote improved weight and health outcomes.

Keywords: alopecia, GLP-1, poor skin quality, skin sagging, volume loss, weight loss

## What is known about this subject in regard to women and their families?

- Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists have become increasingly utilized in obesity care, and women comprise a large number of patients navigating weight management.

- Aesthetic, dermatologic, and muscle sequelae of patients treated with this pharmacotherapy for weight management have not been systematically evaluated by board-certified dermatologists in collaboration with weight management physicians.

## What is new from this article as messages for women and their families?

- Our study explores patient-reported dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic concerns among patients using glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists.

- Our study offers a preventive, holistic approach to nutrition, strength preservation, and aesthetic and dermatologic therapies to optimize weight and health outcomes for patients undergoing treatment with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists.

## Introduction

The term “Ozempic face” has become emblematic of facial volume changes thought to be secondary to glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) use.1 Despite increasing recognition in social and clinical contexts, data on the prevalence and impact of dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic effects remain limited.

This study, which evaluates patient-reported dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic outcomes among individuals treated with weight management pharmacotherapy, informs prevention and management approaches. By emphasizing nutritional optimization, strength preservation, early dermatologic evaluation, and potential intervention, we propose integrating a preventive holistic framework that optimizes dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic outcomes into the overall algorithm of weight management treatment.

## Materials and methods

This institutional review board–approved study utilized a voluntary, anonymous survey developed based on qualitative interviews with weight management physicians and dermatologists treating dermatologic concerns associated with weight management. This survey was made available in April-May 2025 to individuals receiving weight management treatment through a national telemedicine platform. Data collected included current weight management therapies: medication type, dosage, and duration, as well as pre-treatment and current body weight. Participants responded to qualitative items regarding dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic outcomes associated with weight management therapy, such as changes in pre-existing skin conditions, emergence of new conditions, and perceived changes in skin quality, hair, nails, facial appearance, and body composition.

Study data were collected and analyzed using Research Electronic Data Capture. A targeted literature review using PubMed was conducted to identify evidence-based strategies for preventing and managing the most frequently reported dermatologic and aesthetic effects. These findings were synthesized into a practical framework for use in dermatologic practice.

## Discussion

In this survey of over 1,200 individuals undergoing medical weight management, aesthetic, muscle, and dermatologic concerns were common. Participants who achieved >20% TBWL reported higher rates of concerns compared with those achieving <10% TBWL, suggesting a dose-response relationship. Concerns were more frequent among patients treated with GLP-1-RAs.

### Skin sagging

Skin sagging, particularly of the arms (71%, n = 390), was the most frequently reported concern. Weight loss limits the skin’s adaptive capacity, leading to laxity in the face, neck, arms, abdomen, and thighs. Loss of elastin, collagen, and subcutaneous fat produces wrinkles, folds, and drooping that diminish aesthetic gains and may cause functional limitations.2,3

Nonsurgical options for mild to moderate laxity include radiofrequency (RF), high-intensity focused ultrasound, fractional lasers, and fractional RF microneedling, which stimulate collagen and elastin synthesis to improve firmness and elasticity with minimal downtime.4–6

### Decreased facial volume

Nearly one third of participants reported facial volume loss, particularly among those with >20% weight loss and on GLP-1-RAs. The most affected regions are typically the midface, temples, and periorbital area, where subcutaneous fat depletion produces a hollow, aged appearance.1,3 Researchers hypothesize GLP-1RAs cause a loss of protective cytokines, increase oxidative stress, and promote adipose-derived stem cell death.7

Treatment includes dermal fillers and biostimulatory agents such as poly-L-lactic acid and calcium hydroxylapatite to promote longer-term collagen production. Early initiation of poly-L-lactic acid during medical weight management may help prevent progression of volume loss.8

### Alopecia

Alopecia was reported by 29% of participants, particularly among those with >20% weight loss and on GLP-1RA therapy. While GLP-1RAs may improve scalp perfusion, they may also disrupt the follicular cycle, contributing to telogen effluvium.9 Nutritional deficiencies and caloric restriction further exacerbate shedding.10 Conversely, there is evidence to suggest GLP-1RAs mitigate inflammation and fibrosis in central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia, thus improving clinical outcomes for these patients.11

Alopecia often improves with nutritional recovery and weight stabilization in patients with telogen effluvium, although data in GLP-1RA users are lacking. Preventive strategies include adequate protein and micronutrient intake, as well as topical or oral minoxidil. For patients with androgenetic alopecia, 5α-reductase and androgen receptor blockade can be considered after discussion with their physician about other considerations (eg, possible side effects). Early initiation of platelet-rich-plasma therapy can be recommended for high-risk patients.12–14

### Worsened skin quality

Approximately one fourth of participants reported worsened skin quality, most often dryness with new fine lines and wrinkles, particularly among those with >20% weight loss. Contributing factors might include reduced hydration from medication-related thirst suppression, and protein or micronutrient deficits during weight loss. Dehydration and micronutrient deficiencies – including depletion of water-soluble vitamins such as vitamin C and copper (its deficiency implicated in genodermatoses with premature aging) – can have a compounded effect that compromises hydration, collagen synthesis, and barrier function, leading to xerosis, poor healing, and reduced elasticity.15–19 Histologic studies following massive weight loss (38-68 kg) have demonstrated epidermal thinning, disorganization of collagen, and fragmentation of elastic fibers.20,21

Prevention focuses on nutritional optimization to ensure adequate fluid and protein intake and to avoid nutritional deficiencies. Additional management may include use of retinoids, antioxidants, microdepot hyaluronic acid injections (United States Food and Drug Administration-approved to improve skin smoothness), and energy-based procedures such as lasers, microneedling, and RF.15,22

### Decreased muscle strength

Eighteen percent of participants reported decreased muscle strength, mostly involving the extremities. While GLP-1RAs primarily reduce fat mass, 15-25% of weight loss is lean tissue; however, volume loss is not reflective of function or strength.23,24 Lean tissue loss may be exacerbated by rapid weight reduction, inadequate protein intake, and insufficient resistance training. Excessive muscle depletion raises risks for sarcopenia, functional decline, and even longevity, with low thigh muscle strength predicting poorer survival.16,25

Preservation requires optimizing nutrition and resistance training, particularly targeting the thigh muscles.23,25 Adjunctive energy-based technologies such as high-intensity focused electromagnetic therapy can improve muscle tone.16,26,27 Early preventive measures are essential to maintain muscle strength and function during weight loss.

This study highlights the importance of anticipating potential dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic sequelae of medical weight management, particularly in the setting of significant TBWL, as these concerns can affect weight and health outcomes. A multidisciplinary approach is essential to balance metabolic and aesthetic goals. Collaboration among obesity medicine specialists, dietitians, and medical and cosmetic dermatologists facilitates early identification of at-risk patients and implementation of preventive measures.

Foundational measures include proactive counseling, adequate protein intake, micronutrient sufficiency, hydration, and resistance exercise. Dermatologic and aesthetic interventions include procedural options like energy-based therapies, fillers, and platelet-rich-plasma, in addition to retinoids, antioxidants, emollients, and topical and oral minoxidil (Table 2).

## Conclusion

While medical weight management offers significant health benefits, it is frequently accompanied by aesthetic, muscle, and dermatologic concerns that can limit adherence to treatment. As the use of GLP-1-RAs expands and patients can achieve greater TBWL, aesthetic, muscle, and dermatologic impacts will become more prevalent. A holistic approach to caring for these patients, inclusive of their dermatologic, muscle, and aesthetic needs, is necessary to promote greater weight and health outcomes.

## Introduction

Inﬂammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, immune-mediated disease of the gastrointestinal tract comprised of two main subtypes, ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn’s disease (CD). Patients with IBD often continue to experience abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, and bloating despite disease remission, now termed IBD with Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)-like symptoms (1). The mechanisms of this relationship have remained elusive, with possible post-inﬂammatory visceral hypersensitivity, microbiome changes, dysregulated gut-brain interactions, intestinal permeability, and/or immune activation at play (1). The presence of IBS-like symptoms in IBD is associated with worse quality of life and increased psychological distress (1–3), potentially on par to the impacts of active IBD (2). Disentangling these entities is crucial to prevent unnecessary escalation or discontinuation of therapies for patients with symptoms that do not represent IBD disease activity (4) and provide more targeted treatment. Estimates of the prevalence of IBS-like symptoms in IBD have ranged widely due to difﬁculty measuring IBS in the IBD population and the changing deﬁnitions of IBS. A systematic review and metaanalysis of 27 observational studies found a pooled prevalence of IBS in IBD of 32.5% (5), substantially higher than the IBS rate of about 6% observed in the general population (6). However, the prevalence of IBS in IBD varied according to how remission was deﬁned, with lower rates observed when endoscopic data was utilized (5). More recently, a prospective analysis utilizing concurrent IBS symptom and endoscopic evaluation found a much lower rate of IBS in IBD compared to prior studies (7.9% by Rome IV criteria and 15.2% by moderate-to-severe IBS-Symptom Severity Score), suggesting that when strict criteria are used, IBS-like symptoms in IBD may be less common than was previously thought (7). Beyond prevalence estimates, the clinical implications of IBSlike symptoms in the course of IBD remain unclear. Only two studies from a cohort in the United Kingdom (UK) have explored this question, ﬁnding that IBD patients with IBS-like symptoms had greater HCU but did not have worse longitudinal disease outcomes over time (2, 8). These studies, however, had limited ability to distinguish IBS-like symptoms from IBD since they lacked endoscopic data and utilized a suboptimal fecal calprotectin (FCP) cutoff of 250 ug/g (9) to deﬁne quiescent IBD. The aim of this study was therefore to utilize a cohort of patients with IBD and evaluation of IBS-like symptoms by concurrent symptom and endoscopic evaluation to determine the longitudinal impacts of IBS-like symptoms in IBD.

## Materials and methods

## Study design and population

This was a single-center study of a longitudinal retrospective followup of a prospectively recruited cohort at a tertiary care academic medical center (7). Adults aged 18 and older with established IBD were approached at the time of index colonoscopy (between 2020 and

2022) to complete study questionnaires including demographic and baseline clinical data. Participants completed the IBS-Severity Scoring System (IBS-SSS), a validated tool for studying IBS-like symptoms in IBD (10). Patients with quiescent IBD, deﬁned as endoscopic remission (endoscopic Mayo score 0 or 1 for UC and no ulcerations for CD) at the index colonoscopy (11), were stratiﬁed into three groups: no IBS-like symptoms (IBS-SSS score <75), mild IBS-like symptoms (IBS-SSS score 75-175), and moderate-severe IBS-like symptoms (IBS-SSS score >175). Clinical data through 9/30/2025 were then manually extracted from the electronic medical record by two physicians ([SM], [AS]). A third physician ([AC]) was available for consultation to resolve questions or discrepancies as needed. Patients were excluded if they did not achieve a minimum follow-up time of 90 days after index colonoscopy.

## Study outcomes

The primary outcome was total IBD-related healthcare utilization (HCU), deﬁned as the total number of IBD-related HCU events including IBD-related clinic visits, endoscopic and imaging evaluations, emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and surgeries until the end of follow up. IBD-related clinic visits were deﬁned as visits with a gastrointestinal specialist regarding symptoms. This included both regular scheduled follow-ups and additional appointments due to symptom burden. All subsequent endoscopic evaluations and any imaging (including CT, MRI, CT enterography or MR enterography) obtained with the purpose of evaluating IBD disease activity within the study period were also included. Emergency department visits and hospitalizations were judged to be IBD-related if gastrointestinal symptoms were thought to be due to IBD disease activity. IBD-associated conditions such as venous thrombosis as well as complications of IBD medications were also included. The HCU could be physician or patient driven. A secondary outcome was time to unscheduled/acute HCU deﬁned as imaging evaluations, emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and surgeries. IBD-related clinic visits and endoscopic evaluation were excluded, as these are part of the standard of care for monitoring IBD. Another secondary outcome was time to treatment failure deﬁned as drug discontinuation due to primary non-response, loss of response, or serious adverse event and was evaluated only among patients receiving biologics at baseline.

## Statistical analysis

Qualitative data are presented as counts and percentages, and quantitative data are presented as median (interquartile range [IQR]). Continuous and categorical variables were compared between groups using the Kruskal-Wallis test and the chi-square or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate, respectively. A generalized linear model with a negative binomial distribution using log follow-up time as an offset was performed to model the number of HCU events based on IBS-like symptoms and provide adjusted incidence rate ratio (aIRR) adjusting for IBD type and biologic therapy at baseline. A time-to-event survival analysis was performed for unscheduled/ acute HCU and treatment failure using Kaplan-Meier curves. Patients were followed from the time of the index colonoscopy until HCU or treatment failure or the end of follow up. The proportional hazards

## Discussion

In this single-center cohort of patients with quiescent IBD, we demonstrated that IBS-like symptoms were independently associated with greater HCU over a median follow-up of 3.5 years. After adjusting for IBD type and biologic therapy, mild and moderate/ severe IBS-like symptoms were associated with unscheduled/acute HCU. As shown in Table 2, the excess HCU was driven mainly by imaging rather than endoscopies, which were proportionally higher in the group without IBS symptoms, or hospitalizations and emergency visits, which were few. This along with the possibility of surveillance bias and the fact that patients with IBS symptoms had more anxiety and depression may explain the higher rates of HCU in this population compared to patients without IBS symptoms. These ﬁndings build upon prior work by leveraging concurrent endoscopic and symptom evaluation to more rigorously characterize the longitudinal impacts of IBS-like symptoms in IBD. Our ﬁnding that IBS-like symptoms are associated with increased HCU is consistent with two prior studies from a UK cohort which similarly identiﬁed greater healthcare use among IBD patients with IBS-like symptoms (2, 8).
